Kicking the Habit: Sports as a Path Out of Drug Abuse in Sierra Leone

A comprehensive community-based initiative using the power of football — and sport — to reclaim the lives of young Sierra Leoneans.

Location: Freetown, Sierra Leone Duration: 3-month Programme Reach: 200+ Direct Beneficiaries Focus: Youth Aged 12–17

Sierra Leone's youth carry the promise of a nation still healing from civil war. Yet for many, the promise is buried beneath cycles of substance abuse, poverty, and trauma — with nowhere to turn and no path forward.

Over 60% of Sierra Leone's population is under 25. In the capital Freetown, entire communities — Congo Town, Kroo Bay, Susan's Bay, and others — watch their young people disappear into addiction to marijuana, alcohol, and the devastating synthetic drug known as "kush." Even school-attending students are not immune: many who sit in classrooms by day face intense pressure from drug-using peers, poverty, and trauma outside school hours. Traditional interventions have fallen short. What is urgently needed is something different: something that meets young people where they are, speaks the language they love, and gives them a reason to choose another path.

That something is sport.

A member at Youth Sport Development SL visits a school, engaging students during a classroom session in Freetown, Sierra Leone.

01

The Crisis Facing Sierra Leone's Youth

The aftermath of Sierra Leone's civil war (1991–2002) created deep social wounds that have never fully healed. Poverty, unemployment, family breakdown, and unprocessed trauma have left a generation of young people profoundly vulnerable. Without recreational facilities, educational opportunities, or positive role models, many turn to substances as a means of escape.

The consequences ripple outward: increased crime, school dropout, deteriorating health, social displacement, family disintegration, and reduced economic productivity. Critically, the crisis does not stop at the school gate — students who remain enrolled are frequently exposed to substances within their communities and peer networks, putting their academic futures and wellbeing at serious risk.

85% of affected youth use marijuana
45% use synthetic "kush" drugs
70% are school dropouts
80% are unemployed
60% suffer depression or anxiety
Members at Youth Sport Development SL during a school outreach session with attending students. Students at school receive substance awareness information from volunteers at Youth Sport Development SL.

Risk factors compound one another: 90% come from low-income families, 65% from single-parent or broken homes, and 55% have direct experience of war or violence. Freetown has only two rehabilitation facilities to serve the entire city. The gap between need and response is vast.

02

Wahab Jalloh's Story: From Addiction to Leadership

To understand why this programme matters, you need only know Wahab Jalloh.

Case Study

Wahab Jalloh, 19 — Congo Town, Freetown

Wahab Jalloh began using marijuana at 14 after dropping out of school due to poverty. His father was killed during the civil war, leaving his mother to support five children through petty trading. Surrounded by peers who used substances and with no positive alternative, he escalated to daily use of multiple drugs — including kush — over three years. He stole to fund his addiction, became homeless, and was completely estranged from his family.

"I watched my son disappear before my eyes," his mother recalled. "The boy who once helped me at the market became someone I didn't recognise."

His turning point came when a community outreach worker introduced him to a local football club that worked with troubled youth. What followed was a transformation in three phases:

Engagement

Initially resistant, Wahab Jalloh was drawn in by the non-judgmental atmosphere. Informal football sessions began to reduce his drug use as his body demanded more.

Commitment

He joined structured training, began counselling sessions, and formed genuine bonds with coaches and teammates. His physical and mental health improved visibly.

Transformation

Wahab Jalloh became team captain, completed a rehabilitation programme, reconciled with his family, enrolled in adult education, and began coaching younger children.

Two years on, Wahab Jalloh is drug-free for 18 months, employed as a youth sports coordinator, studying for his secondary school certificate, living with his family — and now mentoring other at-risk youth in his community.

Mr. Geogle Floodie (right) works alongside a member of Youth Sport Development SL — the kind of intergenerational mentorship at the heart of the programme.

Wahab Jalloh's story is not an isolated miracle. It is a proof of concept — and the foundation upon which this programme is built.

03

Why Sport Works

Football is not simply a game in Sierra Leone — it is a national language. It transcends social, economic, and cultural boundaries. Sports-based interventions have demonstrated success in post-conflict societies worldwide, and the evidence base is clear:

🏃

Structure & Purpose

Regular training gives young people routine, time management, and a reason to show up each day.

🤝

Positive Relationships

Teams replace drug-using peer networks with healthy bonds, mentorship, and belonging.

💪

Confidence & Discipline

Athletic achievement builds self-esteem, goal-setting skills, and resilience under pressure.

🌱

Healing & Release

Physical activity provides a healthy outlet for stress, trauma, and emotional pain.

The combination of physical activity and counselling proved more effective than either approach alone. Community acceptance and family reconciliation were crucial for sustained recovery.

— Programme Findings, based on Wahab Jalloh's Case Study
04

The Programme: A Holistic Approach

This initiative operates across four integrated components, designed to address not just symptoms but the root causes of youth drug abuse.

Sports Training and Development sits at the core — daily training in football, basketball, athletics, and traditional Sierra Leonean sports. Regular inter-community competitions create pride, aspiration, and sustained engagement. Leadership is cultivated deliberately through team captain roles and youth-led decision-making.

Drug Prevention and Education runs alongside every session. Substance awareness, life skills, decision-making, peer resistance strategies, mental health literacy, and financial education are woven into the programme's DNA — delivered in ways that connect culturally and resonate personally.

Counselling and Rehabilitation Support ensures those already affected by drugs receive the care they need. Individual and group counselling, family therapy, psychosocial support for trauma recovery, and medical referrals are all provided. No one is turned away for the severity of their situation.

Community Mobilisation makes the effort sustainable. Traditional and religious leaders, parents, local businesses, and community members are engaged as partners — not just beneficiaries. Youth-led advocacy and peer education create a multiplier effect, spreading the programme's reach well beyond its direct participants.

05

Who We Reach

The programme targets seven communities within Freetown with the highest rates of youth drug abuse: Congo Town, Kroo Bay, Susan's Bay, Dworzark, Wellington, Kissy, and Calaba Town. Future phases will extend to Waterloo, Newton, and beyond.

Programme Reach — Direct and Indirect Beneficiaries

200
At-risk youth, aged 12–17
50
Drug-affected youth in intensive care
400
Family members supported
800
Peers reached through education
50
Community leaders trained
7
Communities in Freetown

Among the direct beneficiaries are both school-attending students at risk of dropping out, and those who have already left — alongside street-connected youth, young people from troubled households, and first-time offenders referred through the justice system. Reaching students while they are still in school is a key prevention priority: intervening early, before substance use takes hold, is far more effective than rehabilitation after the fact. Women and girls — who face unique vulnerabilities including sexual exploitation and cultural restrictions on sports participation — are prioritised through gender-sensitive programming and safe dedicated spaces.

06

A Three-Year Journey

The programme unfolds across four carefully sequenced phases over 3-months, ensuring deep community roots before full-scale rollout.

Foundation & Setup

Community entry, stakeholder engagement, baseline assessments, infrastructure development, staff recruitment and training.

Programme Launch

Youth recruitment and enrolment, sports training begins, counselling services initiate, community education campaigns launch.

Full Implementation & Expansion

Programme scaling, advanced competition, income-generating activities, strengthened community partnerships, mid-term evaluation.

Consolidation & Sustainability

Transfer to community ownership, documentation of best practices, training of local trainers, final impact assessment, replication planning.

08

Partners & Stakeholders

Mr. Geogle Floodie addresses school students during an outreach visit supported by Youth Sport Development SL.

No single organisation can solve this alone. The initiative brings together a broad coalition of partners spanning government, international agencies, civil society, the private sector, and academia.

Government partners include the Ministry of Youth Affairs, the Ministry of Health and Sanitation, the Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education, and the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency. International support comes from organisations including UNICEF, WHO, and UNODC. Local NGOs, religious institutions, community-based organisations, the University of Sierra Leone, and the Sierra Leone Police all play active roles.

This multi-sector approach is essential — because youth drug abuse is not a single problem with a single solution. It is the intersection of poverty, trauma, family breakdown, education gaps, and absent opportunity. Addressing it requires everyone at the table.

The Investment Is in Sierra Leone's Future

Wahab Jalloh's transformation is not a rare exception. It is a demonstration of what becomes possible when a young person is given structure, belonging, support, and a reason to believe in themselves. This programme exists to make that possible — at scale, sustainably, community by community.

Every young person reached is a family restored, a community strengthened, and a future secured.
